title: LedgerRehearsal
about_excerpt: Rehearse before agents act. Like Comment Story Updates Deterministic receivables baseline — Three fictional accounts and three safe agent tools before approval. Approval changes the tool surface — One uniquely scoped execution capability appears after human review. Stale permission disappears — Drift applies nothing and removes the approved execution capability. Exact rehearsal before action — Complete simulated ACME reminder, Jones assignment diff, and Smith policy block. Receipt separates proposed, authorized, executed, and blocked — The final record explains what happened and whether reality changed. Rehearsal against current reality — ACME is no change, Jones remains proposed, and Smith remains blocked. Short description LedgerRehearsal is a WebMCP accounts-receivable demo where a human and an agent review the same exact business transition before the webpage exposes a one-time capability to execute it. If reality changes after approval, the page removes that capability and requires a fresh rehearsal. Inspiration Approval interfaces often live beside an agent rather than inside the interface the agent can actually use. A screen may say “approved” while the agent’s available actions remain unchanged. LedgerRehearsal asks a narrower question: what if the WebMCP tool surface itself became shared interface state between a person and an agent? The project uses a familiar accounts-receivable scenario because the stakes are easy to understand. An overdue reminder may be reasonable when an invoice is unpaid and wrong seconds later if a payment arrives. The interesting moment is not generating the reminder; it is proving that a previously reviewed permission disappears when its factual basis changes. What it does The agent begins with three safe tools: inspect_accounts , propose_collection_actions , and rehearse_transition . The first rehearsal proposes an overdue reminder for ACME, proposes assigning Jones to Maya Chen, and blocks a final notice for Smith because the invoice is disputed. The human reviews the complete simulated message, exact before/after values, effects, and blocked reason in the webpage. Human approval then makes one uniquely named, zero-argument execution capability appear. Before the agent uses it, the human simulates ACME’s payment. That state change invalidates the reviewed transition, so stale execution applies no business mutation, creates no outbox effect or receipt, and removes the capability. The agent rehearses again against current reality. ACME becomes NO_CHANGE , Jones remains PROPOSED , and Smith remains BLOCKED . A second human approval creates a distinct capability. Using it applies only the stored Jones assignment, adds one simulated outbox effect, writes one receipt, and consumes the capability so replay cannot duplicate the change. All customers, balances, messages, and effects are fictional. There is no real email, payment provider, financial API, or external financial operation. How it was built LedgerRehearsal is a React 19 and TypeScript application built with Vinext for Cloudflare Sites. A D1-backed transition store keeps deterministic fictional account state, reviewed manifests, expected account versions, exact typed changes, simulated effects, blocked items, and lifecycle events. The browser uses top-level imperative WebMCP registration through document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , with the current Chrome compatibility path at navigator.modelContext . Each approved execution registration receives an AbortSignal so it can be removed when authorization expires, drifts, or is consumed. The execution tool accepts zero mutation arguments. The agent cannot substitute an account, owner, message, or value after review. On execution, the server claims the transition with compare-and-swap semantics, rechecks stored preconditions, applies only stored after-values, appends simulated effects, and records the receipt. Competing callers observe the transition as no longer available, so exactly one wins inside this application boundary. How LedgerRehearsal uses WebMCP LedgerRehearsal explores the WebMCP tool surface itself as shared interface state. Human approval makes one reviewed execution capability appear; changing business reality removes it; successful use consumes it. The choreography is visible in actual tool enumeration: 3 safe tools → 4 with reviewed execution → 3 after drift → 4 with replacement execution → 3 after consumption Human approval is deliberately not an agent tool. The consequential capability appears only after a person reviews the concrete transition in the webpage. Human-agent collaboration The agent is good at inspecting state, proposing work, and explaining exact effects. The person owns the consequential approval. The webpage connects those roles by changing what the agent can do only after the person reviews a specific transition. That division also makes disagreement legible. Smith is not silently omitted; the rehearsal shows the blocked action and its policy reason. When ACME pays, the system does not reinterpret the old approval. It revokes it and asks the agent and person to review the smaller current transition together. Creativity and ambition The project does not claim a new security primitive. Human approval, dry runs, optimistic concurrency, capability-based security, version checks, and single-use authorization all have prior art. The contest contribution is the shared-page experience: approval, drift, replacement, and consumption are reflected directly in the live WebMCP surface rather than only in a status label. Impact Agents become more useful when people can see not just what they plan to do, but exactly when permission exists, what that permission covers, and why it disappears. The pattern is relevant anywhere a reviewed action can become stale: finance operations, customer support, fulfillment, compliance, and other consequential workflows. Challenges The hardest part was keeping browser capability state, server authorization state, and business state aligned. Removing a tool from the browser is not enough if a stale handle can still reach the server, so the server rechecks the reviewed account versions and lifecycle on every execution. Another challenge was making the scenario comprehensible without hiding the mechanics. The interface exposes exact diffs, complete simulated messages, blocked actions, lifecycle events, outbox effects, and receipts while keeping the main story readable. Accomplishments A real 3 → 4 → 3 → 4 → 3 capability lifecycle in supported WebMCP runtimes. Zero-argument execution tied to a reviewed manifest rather than agent-supplied mutation values. Drift detection that applies zero stale business mutations and creates zero stale effects or receipts. Single-use application-boundary execution with replay and competing-caller coverage. Deterministic fictional data, visible reset, and judge-accessible public deployment with no signup. A 32-test suite covering reg
video_transcript_excerpt: Ledger rehearsal is a web MCP receivables workspace where a human and an agent rehearse consequential business changes together before the web page allows execution. The agent begins with three safe tools. It finds Acme overdue with no reminder, Jones needing a follow-up owner, and Smith in an active billing dispute. The page rehearses exact effects before anything changes. I can read the complete simulated Acme reminder, see Jones move from unassigned to Maya Chan, and see why policy blocks Smith. Approval stays a human web page action. Once I approve this exact review, a uniquely scoped execution capability appears. The tool surface changes from three to four. No reality changes before execution. A visible payment sync records Acme's invoices paid in full. The overdue reminder no longer makes business sense. I approved this when Acme was overdue, but Acme paid before the agent acted. So, the page removes that capability instead of letting the agent use stale approval. Nothing executes. The agent must rehearse against current reality. Acme's reminder is gone. Jones is still valid, while Smith remains blocked because the dispute has not changed. I approve the smaller replacement transition. A new distinct execution capability appears, again changing the page's web MCP surface from three tools to four. The agent supplies no targets or replacement values. The application rechecks current state and applies only the stored Jones assignment. Smith's blocked action never executes. Successful use consumes the one-time capability. It disappears. The tool count returns to three and a replay cannot duplicate the change or simulated effect. The receipt records what was proposed, what the human authorized, what actually executed, what remained blocked, and whether reality changed after rehearsal. Rehearse before agents act. Approval changes what the page lets the agent do. Changing reality revokes that permission.

live_observation.first_impression: Accounts receivable workspace showing three fictional customer accounts, balances, due states, follow-up status, and a simulated outbox.
live_observation.after_state: The app displayed a Preparing the receivables workspace loading state; the proposed-work result was not visible within the observation window.
live_observation.notes: Initial state clearly presents ACME, Jones, and Smith scenarios and a human review entry point.
